comments.name: CaroT
comments.body:
My brother was a member of Chi Phi at Cornell 20+ years ago. I graduated from a large public university and was not in a sorority. I work as a paralegal in a District Attorney’s office.

The debate over whether or not the events described in the original complaint or civil lawsuit would meet the criteria for a rape charge under NYS criminal law and whether or not the law should be changed to protect women who are intoxicated is an important debate. I’m sure it will continue as more information comes to light and hope there are changes that offer greater protection for vulnerable people.

The debate I find maddening is whether or not these guys did something illegal. It is *never* legal to possess a big bag of recreational ketamine. Apparently, Cornell police responded to a ketamine overdose about a week before this incident. Why did the University allow the frat to continue functioning without a real narcotics investigation?

If these elite schools are actually trying to prepare young people for the real world (rather than just raise money from rich donors), maybe they should hold students accountable for serious drug crimes. Turning a blind eye to hard drug use is just a basic administrative failure.

comments.name: Spiro
comments.body:
One could argue that driving a motor vehicle is also a consensual act. The driver chooses to get behind the wheel. But if that driver is intoxicated, the law holds them accountable because their actions can cause harm to others.

The same principle should apply here. If Jane Doe had consented with a clear mind, we could debate the morality of the behavior, but not necessarily its legality.

But in this case, who in their right mind could possibly believe that what happened was acceptable? The moral failure extends beyond the direct participants to the bystanders who witnessed it and did nothing.

To me, there is no question that this was rape. The real question is why the law fails to adequately protect victims in such circumstances, and why we are still debating whether what happened was wrong in the first place.

comments.name: Patricia
comments.body:
While I share the author's belief that these gang bangs are morally reprehensible, I don't think that's enough. The New York state law doesn't take into account that a victim can be both conscious and incapacitated, which is what Jane Doe claims in her suit. The author seems to say that Jane Doe's consent to the initial encounter was consent for everything that happened after it. I disagree. If Jane Doe had never agreed to the initial encounter, but were simply incapacitated by ketamine and alcohol on that young man's bed, would her inability to resist be considered consent? Under New York law, it might.

I think we need state laws that deal with gang rape specifically. If one person, whether male or female, is the object of a pile-on, then there must be affirmative consent from that person for each participant.

He wouldn’t watch “A Christmas Story” after Mom and especially my brother pointed out the similarities of Ralphie’s “Old Man’s” battle with the furnace and the storm windows. Dad stormed right off.

I’m a female. My little ears picked up Dad’s phrasing, spiced with Grandpa’s epithets that made his construction crew blush. I worked with mostly men for 20+ years. New guys would apologize for their language. My crew would laugh and tell them, they were going to learn a lot of new ways to use language. 

An immigrant co-worker was confused by American English’s use of the same word for many things. Nouns, adjectives, homonyms, homophones etc. Bass, desert, dessert. The eph word’s proper usage was particularly perplexing or them: “It’s a noun, it’s an adjective, it’s a verb, how can this be?” The crew made me explain. 

That said, not Dad, not Grandpa, not me nor my coworkers would ever/had ever used this language in formal settings or in public. The occasional exclamation, sure. It’s like arguing that overweight people are drawn to fast food, but fast food has nothing to do with their weight. Or that mental health issues lead to drug use and addiction, while ignoring that drug use itself can contribute to addiction and mental health problems.

The reality is that these relationships work in both directions.

Excessive screen time, particularly when it replaces face-to-face interaction, physical activity, and meaningful social engagement, can contribute to isolation and poor mental health. We cannot simply dismiss those consequences by arguing that inadequate access to mental healthcare is the real problem.

Do we need better access to mental healthcare to treat people experiencing these issues? Absolutely. But shouldn’t we also be addressing the behaviors and environmental factors that may be contributing to those problems in the first place?

Treating the consequences while ignoring potential causes is hardly a sustainable solution.

comments.name: Madeline Jacobson
comments.body: I’d heard about Flock cameras before this, but one thing that surprised me was that the cameras only record license plate numbers - not faces or actions, but license plate numbers. They can only be used to track someone’s location, which is frankly a relief, as it limits the potential abuses of this technology, say, for censorship or blackmail. In theory, they can only be used to actively find criminals, not monitor ordinary people. But the technology’s critics still decry the very nature of the cameras: passively watching anyone who passes by, collecting information just waiting for the wrong person to get ahold of it. Before, invading someone’s constitutionally-promised privacy was a conscious choice. Now, even before a corrupt officer actually uses the data, it’s automatic. I personally believe that this technology can be used for good, but only if it changes from passively surveilling everyone to only searching for people who are actually dangerous - after enough good human beings push the button.

comments.name: Noah
comments.body: I am somewhat concerned with the use of surveillance/flock cameras on the road. As the article highlights, flock cameras are a potentially useful tool for identifying criminals, however, in the wrong hands, these cameras can be utilized for all of the wrong reasons. I personally have encountered multiple examples online of the AI in the cameras making a mistake, causing wrongful traffic stops and arrests. As a result, I am an advocate for a slightly different approach to these flock cameras. I acknowledge that these cameras can be useful, but I argue they should need to be approved by the city that is using them, and any example of a “crime” should be reviewed by the police station, before any action is taken. That way, these cameras can be both properly utilized, and they wouldn’t have to worry about people hating them, and organized groups attempting to tear them down.

comments.name: Omar Aamir
comments.body:
Jeremy Engle uses Neil Vigdor’s work, “Flock Cameras are Dividing  U.S. Cities: Here’s What to Know About Them,” in order to construct a report of the criticisms surrounding the new Flock Safety cameras. US Citizens debate on the usage of these cameras on the fact whether or not they’re lawful. On the supporters’ side, one rationalizes that this surveillance system will help fight crime via tracking criminals. However in contrast to this, critics point out that this is unlawful by violating American’s Fourth Amendment right which disallows unlawful searches without a warrant.  

In my opinion after reading this article, I do agree that this system is unlawful and I am against it although I get the main purpose of it is justified. People detest it reasonably because of how it allows for no privacy- from 75 feet of its surroundings due to its constant scanning. Although in the article, I can see the overall purpose of it with Ryan Routh’s capture which was because of his attempt to assassinate President Trump and his capture being tied back to Flock Cameras. In conclusion, I agree with the stance that Flock Cameras are unlawful and regulations need to be placed on them, but I understand their purpose although it is not being thoughtfully carried out.

comments.name: Owais
comments.body: I have heard of flock cameras before reading this article. In fact, i’ve gathered many contextual information about it on social media but have never thought of going beyond that and searching for actual facts. From the text, I learned that these systems instantly produce a high volume of highly sophisticated surveillance records for law enforcement. The detail from this article that stood out to me the most was Daniel J Stove’s quote, who is a law professor stating “It is a form of a dragnet.”  explaining that thus technology tests the fourth amanendent in ways that the constitutional farmers could never have anticipated. This stood out to me the most because I’ve known this could cause a lot of privacy issues but never once thought to think about the legality of it. Ultimately, this leaves me wondering how citizens can protect the sleeves when the government can just track their movement

comments.name: Trey
comments.body: I am partially concerned about the growing use of Surveillance Technology after considering both the pros and cons. A positive of Surveillance Technology, such as flock cameras is their ability to catch crimes. For example, Neil Vigdor describes that flock cameras have “automated license plate readers that employ artificial intelligence to identify and track vehicles.” Through the use of this advanced technology, government agencies can detect where criminals might be and  where a stolen car is, further limiting the crime occurring in our nation. Despite flock cameras' ability to limit crime, U.S citizens like Daniel J. Solove confidently argue that they are an invasion of privacy, even taking it to an extreme claim: “It is a form of a dragnet”. Americans all over the country value the words written in our amendments, making privacy invasion a huge deal. Also, Solove's argument of an invasion of privacy stems from Flock Safety(owners of the flock camera) being a private company, meaning the valuable information they gather could potentially be in the wrong hands, given that it isn’t just the government who obtains access to it. All in all, my agreement to both arguments presented makes me partially concerned with the growing technology of surveillance.

comments.name: Quentin Hamilton
comments.body: I have seen firsthand the affect surveillance equipment has had on people around me. Many feel like flock cameras are invading our lives by tracking our every move. The CEO of flock said he’s sacrificing privacy for the sake of the country and people were outraged. Now many people destroy flock cameras,or take routes to avoid them. I was concerned about the cameras but now I’m hopeful that more and more people will refuse to accept being surveyed by a private company.

comments.name: Robert Wion
comments.body: Many towns-like the one I live in-have implemented a sort of surveillance system, like flock into the area. And in my personal opinion I have a very large disdain for these cameras. First of all the US is spending millions of dollars on a public surveillance system. These funds could be going to some of the more major problems with the country currently, like the rising cost of homes, or the homelessness crisis. I also question the overall safety it brings to the local areas. In 2025 a Texas police officer illegally used Illinois flock license plate cameras to track a woman who had an abortion. Establishing how flock cameras can constantly track citizens across multiple different states, and how they can illegally be misused by officers or people with power.  I personally believe that the US should get rid of the floc cameras and other surveillance systems, because of the constant tracking, low safety, and public outcry that has come with these being installed.

comments.name: Sophia
comments.body: I harbor a deep hatred for Flock and all the similar companies. These cameras are not safe and I fully support all the opposition efforts and I believe that they are entirely justified. First of all, increased surveillance doesn’t fix crime, it just moves it. All the surveillance does is make normal citizens uncomfortable and force criminals to go down the street where there’s less cameras. Secondly, Flock cameras are not just used to read license plates, they read faces too; there are recorded cases of police officers using the cameras to stalk exes. Concerned tech professionals also question the security of the Flock cameras, finding many vulnerabilities that can be used to obtain the camera’s data. The cameras also cannot be easily removed because they are rented and not owned, therefore if a town decides they don’t want the Flock cameras due to the many issues, they can’t remove them until the contract expires. Flock is a mass surveillance system that exists solely for profit, not safety. Any measures that are used to take down the cameras are completely valid in my eyes.

comments.body: Speaking as a tenured professor, this is an example of the abuse of the tenure system. Tenured professors do not have the right to say or do anything they please. They have freedom of speech within their disciplines. They do not have the right to use their classes as a platform for their personal opinions. They do not have the right to teach anything they want — their courses must be approved by their colleagues and by the administration. Everyone with a job is subject to workplace rules. That includes this tiresome example of professorial entitlement.

comments.body: This type of "activism" disguised as teaching does a disservice to rigorous academic scholarship. I am a psychology researcher who also happens to be a proud Jew and Zionist. Does that mean I'm qualified to teach courses on the conflict in the Middle East, or even Jewish studies? Absolutely not--that is best left to experts in those areas. Our job as researchers and educators is to help students think critically without imposing our own opinions and biases on them. I reserve my activism for outside the classroom--it's completely independent of my research, as it should be.

comments.name: Kate
comments.body:
Another example of the concerted effort to shut down pro-Palestinian speech. The argument that a Haitian specialist should not include Palestine in his teaching is absurd. De Graff's field is linguistics and the role of language in colonization. The thematic link to Palestine is entirely legitimate. I have a PhD in Latin American Literature. When I was in graduate school I took a number of courses that ranged far beyond the country that was the professor's specialty, to include other countries or regions, even some outside of Latin America, that were related to the theme of the course. Parallels between countries and regions are critically important in postcolonial studies.

I have already mentioned this in numerous comments, but it bears repeating. This situation is yet another example of the effects of of Project Esther, a scheme hatched by the same Heritage Foundation that brought us Project 2025. Project Esther is a detailed roadmap for using claims of antisemitism to crush any criticism of Israel and shut down progressive speech in general. It was written not by Jews but by right-wing evangelical Christians. The fact that I have found reason to mention it in so many posts on different situations is a testament to just how ubiquitous its influence is. It needs to be more widely exposed. Here is an excellent NYT article.
https://www.nytimes.com/2025/05/18/us/project-esther-heritage-foundation-palestine.html?searchResultPosition=3

comments.name: Paul
comments.body:
Interest rates don't even come close to explaining what's going on.  As the director of Swiss-Re told me in 1999 when I was working with NASA on a story on climate change, "the problem with the American economy is it's based on the fantasy of real estate values.  The first cracks will appear not in prices for housing...but in the insurance industry."  

And so it is.  A friend who owns a franchise for a national title company is laying off half his staff, and doors are closing nation wide.  The crash of 2008 proved the gentleman at Swiss-Re correct. Prices dropped 80% in some markets.  Prices don't drop that far when the value is baked into the property.  Nowhere is that fantasy more painful than in California.  A friend of mine just got his new insurance bill...$180,000.  A year!   Flood, fire, earthquakes.  Up 500% year over year.  Fast shift to Florida.  You can't get insurance in Florida.  20,000 residential properties are currently for sale in the sunshine state.  No insurance company will touch them...

So the dominos shake and tremble.  The mortgage companies have no paper moving through their offices, which means the banks, which depend on all of that 'free money' from home buyers every month, are starting to make a 'giant sucking sound.'   I wrote that story in 1999. Absolutely no one wanted to believe it.  The way no one wanted to believe commercial airliners could be flown into the twin towers.  

Welcome to Disneyland.

It is worth noting that the % of households who own a home has remained relatively steady at 66-67% for decades.  Higher interest rates today compared to the abnormally low 3-4% of recent years is striking, but neither level has moved the needle up or down by much. This fact rarely gets referenced in these types of articles.  

What might be a more compelling topic, and is occasionally noted, is how higher costs in general (eg., insurance, health care, education) are impacting the creation of wealth and financial security of our younger population. That is the bigger and more troubling development over the past 20 years.

But you couldn't learn "corporate" IT back then; computer science was focused on Unix mainframes, programming, or electrical engineering. Such kids start algebra and geometry in 6th grade, trig in 7th and often calculus in 10th - even the artsy types. comments.body:
Two distinct pleasures came in this article.  

(1) Reading about a book by a celebrated author
(2) Reading what other people said about that book.

Because first things first. The only thing I've read by John Steinbeck is "Travels with Charley."  And oh yes!

--there's a short story called "Flight."  Which I read in high school.  About a young man whose business took him to some town in the southwest--

--where he fought with and killed another man.  He comes back home with the bad news.  He's on the run--

--but no matter!  It's all up with him. His days are numbered.  

And so--

--he hightails it into the wilderness .  There are pursuers on his trail.  And eventually--exhausted, out of options!  he stands up on a lonely hilltop.  A single shot rings out.  And--

--you get the idea.  A marvelous tale!  Gripping I call it.    

Which leaves "East of Eden."  

I was struck by a comment that compared Mr. Steinbeck favorably with Shakespeare and Faulkner.  Well, the bard wrote four centuries ago.  And yes, parts of Shakespeare are heavy going.  

But Faulkner?  My stars, yes!  Faulkner can be very heavy going.  Which I gather is not true of Steinbeck.  Someone used the word "flat" to describe his writing--

--and that's of a piece with my own experience.

'Cause there are authors that hold forth and pontificate--

--and those that recount what they had to recount--

--and let the story do the rest.  And so--

--I can't wait to get into "East of Eden." 

Thanks, NYT.

After more than 20 years in France, and 20 more dealing with French people professionally, I have come to a conclusion.
France has been a nation in the wider sense for more than 500 years. 
It is highly centralised and wants to be culturally uniform. Regional languages, for example, were long suppressed and are still barely tolerated.
The state is overwhelming and demands control in every aspect of life. The scope of regulations is mindboggling.
The French still need to live their lives and have responded by a mixture of obedience, ignoring the rules if they feel like it, and by occasional rebellious acts that can border on insurgency.
They cannot ignore the overwhelming state and its outrageous bureaucracy but they also like the certainty it provides. There is no situation in life where the French state would no involve itself. And that's how every French citizen has been brought up.
Nowadays the French state is failing. 
It has no answers to climate change which means endless floods in winter and burning forests in summer. 
It can't stop imports which are wiping out French manufacturing which is far too expensive because the state taxes labour massively. 
It has no answers other than bribing the groups that scream the loudest and that are the most violent. 
But is has to borrow this money and that is now hitting the brick wall.
What do you do when your provider abandons you? You lash out in anger and fear. And that's what's happening.

However, it was not Lichtenstein's place to do this, but rather, DC or Marvel, or whatever company paid him for piecework, and owned his production. Even the most successful comic artists of Heath's era, (like Kirby and Toth), struggled with the New York 'sweatshop' production  model of the comic book business at that time, and to varying degrees of success, attempted to find more lucrative new production models in adjacent entertainment fields. Sadly, I suspect Heath's economic struggles in old age were the most common outcome of that profession in the mid 20th century in America. To blame Lichtenstein for this, is short sighted.

David Renard Editor for culture coverage · Thanks for your remark. Because Lichtenstein was making an artistic statement in his work by lifting an image from a comic elsewhere is hardly the point and IMHO not worth mentioning. He wasn't quoting Van Gogh or Goya after all. He used industrial illustrations as his medium and not specifically quoting them per se. At all. In fact, the point he was making was commenting on industrial design that was becoming if not already - an overwhelming presence on the American capitalist scene. Jasper Johns did it, even some Rauschenberg. But Warhol I think you would have to say 'Trumped' them all. cept he rode a wave that led to The Factory and itself became a cultural lab of sorts. Where the truth or the statement was often invisible or unheard or unspoken - when he made thos films and took silent movies of visiting luminaries like Dylan and Jim Morrison. Kind of a moment in time of melding folk art and high art. Almost, dare I say, like a Camelot w/Sedgwick as Guinevere  - until W was shot by deranged Valerie Solanas (of all people- seeing W as some kind of male chauvinist was really misplaced anger). Jus' sayin' 
Artistic Director
The Great American Play Series

comments.name: David
comments.body: Arguments evaluating comic book illustration's art worthiness owe a debt to Lichtenstein. It was discussions regarding Pop Art and his work in particular, which moved western culture's aesthetic goalposts enough to consider commercial illustration as being Art.  That idea was laughable until Pop. Leading up to Lichtenstein's time, comic book drawings (and writing) were predominately published unsigned, or signed pseudonymously, because of the low cultural evaluation of such work, which after all, was only produced to attract the cash of an uneducated mass audience. Lichtensteins real trick was to turn such anonymous hack work into a subject, in which individuals could then be evaluated as better or worse artists.

Anne Carson is my favorite living poet, and I would be remiss if I didn't share some of her other works. "Nox" is incredibly moving and such a beautiful object to hold in one's hands; "Eros the Bittersweet" was so insightful. However, despite their technical brilliance, I never really enjoyed "The Beauty of the Husband" or "The Autobiography of Red."

I would recommend "Men in the Off Hours" and "Decreation." The poems are shorter, even when there is a cycle of poems it is digestible. Carson can be overwhelming, so I like the small doses, where I walk away with a sense of wonder and curiosity about the world. I must have read "Sleepchains" a hundred times without ever fully understanding it, but every time I read it, I get goosebumps and a visceral sensation of distance, worry, and anticipation.

(And I might give "The Beauty of the Husband" and "The Autobiography of Red" another try. It's been over a decade... things hit differently at different ages.)

As a teenager, I volunteered at Highgate Cemetery, an overgrown mass of ivy and oak scattered with weeping angels. Much of the site was out of bounds, the ground so riddled with roots and burials that it was liable to collapse.

London is like this — layer upon layer of history; buildings once one thing, now another. And on every corner: stories. Here are the docklands of Dorian Grey, the heart of empire and its evils. Here is Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde’s Soho, a den of vice turned tourist trap. Here is Piccadilly, where Dracula kept a townhouse; here, Hampstead Heath, where Wilkie Collins’s woman in white once walked.

This is how I grew up, in a city constantly reimagining itself — full of ghosts, and their tales.

Why are we so compelled to retell stories, especially the frightening ones? Perhaps it is the hope of safety, that this time we can change the ending. But a retelling is not a safe thing at all. It is an act of reinvention and distortion — a fresh way into old horrors, or an old lens on a new nightmare.

Mildly surreal to see Sokoban on the front page of the NYT website. One of the original games licensed here, Skipping Stones to Lonely Homes, was a major gateway into the genre for me when it came out, and I highly recommend people seek it out (along with other work by Hazelden's studio) for a simple and accessible intro into this sort of puzzle game.

Having played OotSS for a bit, I'm not won over by the "upgrade" here yet. The movement feels clunky and slow, and typically puzzle games benefit from simple elegance over noise graphically. Also, developers bragging 100+ hour lengths is more of a red flag to me than a selling point.

Would love to see a profile of Jack Lance at some point (who worked on this game). He died at a tragically young age, but his work had an immense impact on the scene in just a few short years.

I am a puzzle game fan and I love Jonathan Blow's games. I appreciate that he's not afraid of making hard puzzles where you have to think several steps ahead, and his puzzle platformer game Braid doesn't have "puzzles" that are secretly platforming challenges like many (and easier) puzzle platformers do. As this article points out, they're really about exploring mechanisms in depth, which is what a true puzzle lover is looking for. The Witness was my favorite puzzle game for a long time, and my friends who I tried getting to play it (and who did not like it) I feel like just didn't have the patience or appreciation of a system that all works together that you really have to learn piece by piece. I am so excited to try this new game.

And I'm saddened to learn from this article that Blow is a Trump fan :(

comments.name: J
comments.body: "Puzzle game" from the guy who made The Witness does not bode well. A large percentage of the puzzles in the Witness were drawing a line around a grid so the path meets certain requirements (i.e. the the path always runs under/over certain colored squares). The problem was, it was obvious the designer drew the paths first, then placed the requirements afterwards. Meaning that MANY of these puzzles had more than one solution. The problem was, the game didn't honor multiple solutions, so you were forced to guess which path the designer intended. Once or twice could have been chalked up to one of those things. But it keeps happening over an over. So you're left with a puzzle game created by a really lazy designer. If they're not putting in the work, why should I?

comments.name: Norman
comments.body:
I'm an older guy--

--I turned seventy seven in August.  

And I don't follow modern literature the way I should.  

But I'm delighted for Ms. Carson.  Because--

(1)--okay, I'll admit it.  She's a woman.  And I think women
      right now could use a bit of encouragement.

(2)--she's a Canadian.  And Canada (buffeted, insulted by
      her boorish neighbor) could use a bit of encouragement. 

(3)--and hey!  She's a classicist.  And I'm a classicist. 
       Endeavoring to keep up my Greek and Latin.

I picked up on this last from your opening paragraph.  The Peloponnesian War as recounted by Thucydides?  And the opening line of that massive history?  

My goodness! 

Stuff I don't often run into (meaning no offense) in the pages of The New York Times!  But apart from that--

--how to say this?  

--she doesn't have a blurry mind.  What I mean is--

--poems and essays replete with blurs.  The words sprawling as it were on a page.  But when I try and discern the thoughts, the images behind those words--

--I get a blur.  More words.  Self-referential words.  Stuff that means nothing but itself--

--and boy!  I did NOT get that sense from what you quoted.  Notably the picture of Geryon (!) sitting there, fiddling with a camera.  Because--

--"he'd relinquished speech."  

Talk about a devastating precision! 

And ditto the bit about the squirrel.  And the bored lover, straying off after four years.  And--

--oh, lots of stuff!  

Everything.  

Thanks, NYT.

On top of that, the EU is now facing two trade wars and one active war, along with an influx of migrants that is empowering the rise of both the far right and the far left.

China, on the other hand, is facing slowing economic growth and unemployment pressures. Exports are one of the key factors it can rely on right now. But this time, China is eating into the market share of Europe, Japan, and North America by exporting more value-added goods, including semiconductors, EVs, and renewables — sectors the EU sees as central to its competitiveness.

I think although its not advantageous, but the EU probably doesn't want to escalate, and China doesn't want to play hardball either.

comments.body: As I wrote yesterday in another comment section on Carson's win, New Directions is arguably the best publisher in the US. For its entire existence it has published nothing but distinguished writing. Its list is an education in world literature. From the start it has brought us astounding new writers, important reissues of neglected writers, and slews of great books in translation from around the world. If I see ND on the spine of a book, I look at that book. Every time. More often than not, I acquire it. My debt of gratitude to ND is huge; it has been an beloved companion of my life for decades. Thank you all at ND. How lucky we all are that the visionary James Laughlin created the press, changing the literary landscape in this country forever.
